sentences.text: Allodaposuchus generally possessed a short, flattened, and rounded skull.
The largest known specimen of this animal was approximately 3.7 meters long.
However, the species A. precedens has been estimated to reach a length of 7 meters, or 23 feet.
The species A. hulki possessed large cranial sinuses not found in any other living or extinct crocodilian, which may have aided in hearing out of water and lightening the skull.
This individual also had well-developed muscle attachment points on its scapula, humerus, and cubitus that would allow it to maintain a semi-upright posture suitable for moving on land.
The species A. hulki is named after the Marvel Comics character Hulk due to bone features suggesting strong muscles.
A. hulki possessed large, unique skull sinuses that may have aided hearing out of water and lightened the skull.
Well-developed muscle attachments on its forelimb bones would have allowed a semi-erect stance suitable for walking on land.
The type species A. precedens was named by Hungarian paleontologist Franz Nopcsa in 1928 from fossils found in Vălioara, Romania.
A. subjuniperus was named in 2013 based on a skull found in the Conquès Formation in Huesca, Spain.
A. palustris was described in 2014 from fossils found in the Fumanya Sud locality in the southern Pyrenees.
A. hulki was named in 2015 from fossils found in the Casa Fabà locality within the Tremp Formation.
Remains of A. hulki were found in sediments likely formed in ephemeral ponds within a large floodplain far from permanent water bodies.
Therefore, A. hulki may have spent most of its time out of water, traveling between these ponds in search of food.
Allodaposuchus is generally classified as a non-crocodylian eusuchian crocodylomorph but is sometimes placed among the earliest true crocodylians.
Allodaposuchus belongs to the clade and family Allodaposuchidae.
Early phylogenetic studies concluded that Allodaposuchus was a close relative of modern crocodilians but excluded it from Crocodylia, the group including all modern crocodilians.
A 2010 phylogenetic analysis supported placing Allodaposuchus within Alligatoroidea, a group of crocodilians that includes modern alligators and Leidyosuchus.
Inclusion of postcranial skeletal characters from A. palustris in a 2014 study supports a position within Crocodylia for the genus Allodaposuchus, separating it from Hylaeochampsidae.
Allodaposuchus lived in southern Europe during the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous, and possibly the Santonian stage, spanning from 85.7 to 66 million years ago.
Fossils of Allodaposuchus are known from Romania, Spain, and France.
Fragments of A. precedens were found in the Hațeg Basin dating to the late Maastrichtian stage, just at the end of the Late Cretaceous.
The exact phylogenetic placement of Allodaposuchidae remains disputed among researchers, and the precise membership of the genus Allodaposuchus is currently disputed.
Some studies have suggested that Allodaposuchus is a nomen dubium because the original material is too fragmentary.

In 2016, A. subjuniperus was moved to the genus Agaresuchus because researchers considered it distinct from A. precedens, though Blanco's 2021 study questioned the separation of Agaresuchus and proposed it be treated as a junior synonym of Allodaposuchus.
